papers.title: Transcranial temporal interference stimulation increases slow waves during human NREM sleep
papers.abstract: Slow waves are a hallmark of sleep homeostasis and a target for enhancing restorative sleep. Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) can non-invasively deliver a low-frequency envelope to deep targets and has been shown to increase spectral slow-wave activity during sleep. It remains untested whether tTIS also alters discrete slow waves, how their cortical expression changes, and whether the field each brain receives relates to the response. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, 32 participants received 1 Hz tTIS and 11 a carrier-only control in 3-min episodes targeting the left insula/ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Combining high-density electroencephalography (EEG), source reconstruction and individualized field modeling, we found that tTIS increased slow-wave density by about 20% during and 30% after stimulation, across shallow and deep waves, with limited morphology change. The carrier-only control showed no detected density change. In source space, each wave involved more cortex in both arms, while wave origins did not change. A dose-response analysis showed that tTIS participants who received a stronger modeled field shifted further toward N3 sleep during stimulation, a relation not seen in the control. These results support tTIS as a candidate EEG-compatible tool for modulating slow waves and motivate individualized field modeling to interpret its effects.

papers.title: Mechanistic insights into state-dependent synchronization of neural activity by weak tACS fields
papers.abstract: Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) biases spike timing with weak electric fields, but how recurrent circuitry and network state shape this response is unclear. We simulated tACS in a detailed cortical column model in two network states of varying coherence, roughly corresponding to REM-like and NREM-like states. Despite weak impacts on network firing rates, stimulation entrained network activity at realistically occurring field strengths. Global entrainment was initiated by direct entrainment of ongoing pyramidal cell activity, which subsequently recruited inhibitory interneurons in a state-dependent manner. The NREM-like network locked more strongly to all tested stimulation frequencies, independent of baseline spectral power, and displayed larger recurrent-connectivity-mediated phase lags. However, recurrent connectivity was not required for, and did not amplify, entrainment, but instead produced an offset in baseline network activity. Our results highlight the impact of network state on the response to tACS, and suggest that meso-scale models of electromagnetic-electrophysiological interactions must look beyond single-cell polarization and baseline oscillations at the stimulation frequency.

papers.title: Evidence for correlated evolution of sleep architecture in chronotype populations of Drosophila melanogaster created by artificial selection
papers.abstract: Chronotypes are circadian variants in timing of a behaviour. In humans, some studies have associated differences in sleep timing and quality with underlying circadian clock driven chronotypes although confounding genetic, environmental and social factors complicate the interpretation of these relationships. Here, we present evidence from artificially selected early and late eclosion chronotype populations of Drosophila melanogaster which suggest that divergence in chronotype can lead to correlated evolution of changes in sleep architecture. We find that early chronotype flies exhibit greater sleep fragmentation and shorter sleep latency during night, whereas late flies showed weaker and less consistent changes in the same direction. These differences were broadly seen for both sexes. We also show that environmental cues like temperature cycles can modulate sleep timing and enhance chronotype differences, while increasing light intensity delayed nighttime sleep timing similarly across chronotypes. Additionally, when sleep was disrupted by mechanical perturbations, late flies could not recover lost sleep to the same degree as early and control in a time-of-day dependent manner. In contrast, following simulated jetlag-induced circadian misalignment, early flies showed a greater increase in daytime sleep after phase advances. Our findings suggest that sleep and circadian traits can coevolve, offering insights into the complex interactions between chronotypes and sleep architecture. These populations provide an evolutionary model to investigate how circadian timing, sleep architecture and homeostatic regulation may be linked.

papers.title: Cross-domain competition for memory reactivation resources during sleep
papers.abstract: Targeted Memory Reactivation (TMR) enhances the consolidation of both declarative and procedural memories. As previous research highlights the importance of cross-domain interactions in shaping memory consolidation, we investigated here whether interacting memories from different domains can be co-reactivated by TMR during post-learning sleep, and in turn enhance consolidation. In a fully within-subject design, twenty-four young, healthy participants learned both a motor and an object sequence learning task that were linked or not by a shared ordinal structure. TMR cues associated only with the object task were presented during post-learning non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep which was monitored with electroencephalography (EEG) during a 90-minute nap. We tested whether reactivating object memories would indirectly reactivate the linked motor memory. Behavioral results showed no overall effect of association but indicated that TMR disrupted object memory consolidation without indirectly affecting performance on the linked motor task. Sleep EEG data point to a competition for reactivation resources whereby slow oscillation (SO; 0.5-2 Hz) and spindle activity (12-16 Hz) involved in both memory protection and potentiation during sleep were preferentially allocated to the covert consolidation of the motor trace at the expense of object memory. These findings suggest that cross-domain memories sharing a common learning structure compete for consolidation resources during post-learning sleep.

papers.title: Cycle-based neurostimulation for control of circadian brain network dynamics in human epilepsy
papers.abstract: Biological rhythms modulate symptoms of brain disorders, yet brain stimulation therapies largely overlook the temporal organization of pathological brain states. Harnessing these rhythms could improve therapeutic efficacy. Here, we show that circadian coordination of hippocampal network connectivity is a biomarker of therapeutic response to responsive neurostimulation in epilepsy. Using longitudinal electrocorticography from individuals with bitemporal epilepsy, we find that alignment of circadian connectivity rhythms between the left and right hippocampus predicts seizure reduction. The daily distribution of stimulation also predicts how these rhythms evolve over months. We capture these dynamics using a nonlinear Kuramoto oscillator model and demonstrate that optimizing stimulation timing in silico can improve predicted circadian network alignment. Our findings establish a cycle-based, control-theoretic framework for modelling and potentially reshaping brain network rhythms, offering new opportunities for personalized neurostimulation in epilepsy and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

papers.title: Integrating convolutional variational autoencoders and the Gaussian mixture model for efficient manifold learning and clustering of spatially preserved EEG topographic maps.
papers.abstract: EEG microstate analysis segments continuous brain activity into brief, quasi-stable topographic configurations whose quantity, duration, and transition dynamics index cognitive state and neuropsychiatric conditions. The standard algorithm, modified k-means (ModKMeans), operates in electrode space. It performs hard partitioning, assigning each data point to exactly one cluster, and provides no learned representation, no generative decoder, and no probabilistic soft assignment. In this research, a Convolutional Variational Deep Embedding model (Conv-VaDE) is designed, a topographic-map adaptation of Variational Deep Embedding (VaDE) that places a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) prior on the latent space of a convolutional variational autoencoder and jointly trains the encoder, decoder, and GMM. Microstate polarity invariance, the property that a topography [Formula: see text] and its sign-inverted counterpart [Formula: see text] index the same underlying configuration, is preserved through three coordinated mechanisms: sign-flip augmentation of the training set, a polarity-invariant reconstruction loss, and an encoder regulariser on the latent embedding. The model is evaluated on a sample of healthy participants ([Formula: see text] healthy adults, eyes-closed) from the LEMON resting-state EEG dataset using a multi-quadrant evaluation framework, with each method assessed in its native frame and cross-method comparisons performed via rank-based Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Conv-VaDE instead offers a focused set of capabilities the standard ModKMeans pipeline does not provide: a learned generative latent manifold (silhouette 0.232 at [Formula: see text], with very narrow cross-subject interquartile-range width [Formula: see text] across the 203 participants, indicating highly reproducible latent geometry), decoded GMM cluster centres inspectable as scalp topographies, probabilistic soft assignment for transitional states, and a generative framework supporting downstream representation analysis. A rank-based meta-criterion over silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, and Davies-Bouldin yields modal [Formula: see text] for Conv-VaDE (39.4%) and [Formula: see text] for ModKMeans (29.6%); [Formula: see text] is adopted to align with the canonical Lehmann A/B/C/D literature. Within the classical cluster-validity register, ModKMeans attains a higher silhouette and 4-5 percentage points higher Global Explained Variance at every K (Wilcoxon, BH-corrected, [Formula: see text]). The two methods occupy distinct positions in the methodological design space, with the cross-method comparison characterising the trade-off between direct electrode-space optimisation and learned generative representation rather than adjudicating method superiority.

papers.title: EEG Source Localization with High-Resolution 40-Tissue Head Models: A Comparative Study with MEG during Photic Driving
papers.abstract: While MEG source localization pipelines often employ head models of one single compartment with homogeneous conductivity, researchers and clinicians use at least 3 different layers in head models for EEG source localization. Recent AI-based segmentation makes it possible to generate individualized head models with 40 high-resolution, non-nested tissues. We present a pipeline that can make use of, and test, these highly realistic models for EEG source localization: with the boundary element fast multipole method (BEM-FMM), we compute transcranial electric stimulation (TES) solutions on the full 40-tissue geometry and use them reciprocally to obtain the EEG leadfields. Out approach runs on a single modest workstation, requiring approximately 4.5 min per EEG channel for a mesh of about one million elements at a relative residual of 1e-4. We applied the pipeline to six participants undergoing intermittent photic stimulation at half their individual alpha peak frequency, comparing 61-channel EEG source localizations from 40-tissue and 5-layer models with each other and with localizations from simultaneously recorded MEG. We further compared noiseless synthetic EEG topographies of the two models across the entire cortex. The two models produced highly consistent EEG source localizations (weighed relative difference below 3%), both in close agreement with the MEG localizations within the visual cortex. The synthetic topographies also agreed closely, with differences scaling approximately linearly with the angle between the source orientations of the two models, underscoring the importance of accurate source normals in fixed-orientation source models. These results establish 40-tissue models as a practical and robust basis for EEG source localization, and open the way to applications where nested geometries cannot represent the anatomy, such as infants or patients with skull defects, injuries, or tumors.

papers.title: High-Density EEG Signatures of Cataplexy in Narcolepsy Type 1.
papers.abstract: Cataplexy, the pathognomonic symptom of narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), consists of sudden, emotion-triggered episodes of muscle atonia during wakefulness, with preserved consciousness. Although cataplexy shares features with REM sleep, its neurophysiological nature remains incompletely understood, particularly in humans. We investigated the electrophysiological signature of cataplexy using 128-channels EEG polysomnography in 10 drug-free NT1 adults. We analyzed 73 cataplexy epochs of ~30 seconds from 59 recorded episodes, compared with epochs of quiet wakefulness, N1 sleep, tonic and phasic REM, and direct-entry-REM-sleep. We compared hypnodensity profiles, computed with U-Sleep, of cataplexy and reference states. Regional and topographic spectral power across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands, absolute and relative to total power, were compared across states. EEG fingerprint robustness was assessed via within- and between-participant correlation distances. Cataplexy exhibited a distinct EEG profile with intermediate sleep-wake spectral features. Relative power showed scalp-wide reduced beta and increased delta-theta versus wakefulness, alongside elevated posterior beta and scalp-wide reduced theta-delta versus sleep. Absolute power showed increased global field power across most bands, supporting REM-like activity superimposed onto wake desynchronization. Hypnodensity analysis revealed a mixed-state signature combining wake-, REM-, and N1-like probabilities, supporting a hybrid state. Cataplexy differed from direct-entry-REM-sleep, arguing against a simple wake-to-REM transition. Variability analyses indicated greater between-participants than within-participant differences, suggesting partially conserved but individually expressed EEG signatures. Our findings support that cataplexy is a dissociated hybrid brain state reflecting co-activation of REM-like and wake-like synchronizations, constituting a unique pathological state with intermediate electrophysiological features.

Signatures varied more between than within participants, supporting a dissociated hybrid brain state distinct from direct wake-to-REM transition.

papers.title: Preparatory beta activity reflects the precision demands of an upcoming movement
papers.abstract: Noise and external disturbances continuously push the limb away from its intended path, but not every deviation compromises the goal of an action. The accuracy constraints of a task define the range of acceptable endpoints and thereby set its precision demands, that is, how much noise must be attenuated for the task to succeed. Whether neural activity during movement preparation reflects these precision demands remains largely unexplored. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) while healthy human participants (n = 27) prepared reaching movements toward narrow or wide targets at the same location and with the same timing constraints. An instructed delay before the go cue allowed preparatory activity to be isolated, and mechanical perturbations were applied during movement to probe feedback responses. Narrow targets led to more precise movements, with greater endpoint accuracy, lower variability and smaller perturbation-induced deviations. This was achieved without a reduction in movement speed, and involved greater muscle co-activation and larger long-latency responses to perturbations. Before movement onset, beta power (13-30 Hz) was lower for narrow than for wide targets, an effect that emerged late in the delay period and was concentrated over bilateral parieto-occipital electrodes. In contrast, alpha (8-12 Hz) and theta (4-7 Hz) activity did not differ between conditions. These findings demonstrate that preparatory beta activity is sensitive not only to kinematic requirements of the movement but also the precision with which it must be produced.

papers.title: Heterogeneity of Sleep Complaints at Six Sites from 5 to 3,850 m in China: A Latent Class Analysis.
papers.abstract: Sleep complaints are heterogeneous, and classifying workers simply as good or poor sleepers conceals that heterogeneity. We used latent class analysis to identify sleep phenotypes in a multi-site occupational cohort, to describe their demographic and clinical correlates, and to examine whether reported nocturnal oxygen use at the highest site was associated with subjective sleep. A total of 1236 personnel of a single national employer, each posted to one of six worksites in China at altitudes from 5 to 3850 m, completed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI). Six indicators were entered into a mixed-mode latent class model: five PSQI component scores (subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, sleep disturbance and daytime dysfunction) modelled as ordinal, and the standardized ISI total score modelled as continuous. Solutions with one to six classes were compared on the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria, the sample-size-adjusted Bayesian information criterion, the bootstrap likelihood ratio test, entropy, smallest class size and interpretability, and were checked by repeated split-half estimation. Indicators not recorded at one site were handled by full-information maximum likelihood. Multinomial logistic regression with site fixed effects identified correlates of class membership. Within the highest site, PSQI and ISI scores were compared between participants who did and did not report nocturnal oxygen use. Four classes were identified: no complaints (34.7%), mild (17.2%), moderate (33.5%) and severe multidimensional sleep disturbance (14.6%), with an entropy of 0.885 and mean posterior probabilities of 0.892 to 0.982. The four-class structure recurred in all ten split-half samples and was unchanged when the sparse sleep-efficiency and hypnotic-use components were added. Modelling the same ordinal indicators as Gaussian, by contrast, produced information criteria that declined at every step without identifying a solution. Having at least one chronic condition was the correlate most consistently associated with the disturbed classes (moderate: adjusted odds ratio 2.48, 95% CI 1.38 to 4.47; severe: 3.49, 95% CI 1.81 to 6.73), and habitual snoring was associated with the severe class (2.00, 95% CI 1.34 to 2.97). Class distribution differed across sites, with the disturbed classes most frequent at the coastal and plain sites. Among participants at 3850 m, those not reporting nocturnal oxygen use scored 0.82 points higher on the PSQI (95% CI 0.16 to 1.48) and 1.17 points higher on the ISI (95% CI 0.16 to 2.18) than those who did; the ISI difference lies below the 6-point change regarded as the minimally important difference for that instrument, and class distribution did not differ by reported use. Four sleep phenotypes graded by severity were identified in this cross-sectional multi-site cohort. In these data, a sleep-efficiency component reconstructed without bedtime and rise time was too sparse to inform classification yet able to generate a spurious class, and fitting a Gaussian mixture to the bounded ordinal components left class enumeration undefined. Chronic illness and habitual snoring accompanied the more disturbed phenotypes. Because the highest-altitude stratum comprises a single site, the site differences reported here cannot be separated from site-specific occupational, demographic and screening characteristics and should not be read as effects of altitude; the nocturnal oxygen comparison is observational and exploratory.

papers.title: BDNF-mediated amelioration of sleep disruption-induced behavioral disorders by Ginkgo biloba.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruptions linked to adverse outcomes ranging from cognitive decline (e.g., in memory, learning, and sensory integration) to emotional dysregulation (e.g., stress and pathological anxiety). Although pre-sleep cognitive engagement may alleviate some of these effects, effective pharmacological interventions are needed. Ginkgo biloba, a dietary supplement, exerts broad pharmacological actions that support neural function. Here, we investigate hypothesis that Ginkgo biloba counteracts sleep deprivation's detrimental effects by promoting BDNF-dependent neuroplasticity, thereby restoring cognitive and emotional homeostasis. Twenty-eight male Wistar rats were randomly assigned to four groups: sleep disruption (SD) followed by Ginkgo biloba extract (250 mg/kg i.p.), sleep-disrupted group only, extract only, and control. The Ginkgo biloba collected from botanical garden of Tehran and the extract was prepared via percolation of plant material with ethanol, followed by evaporation and reconstitution. Animals were subjected to multiple-platform-induced sleep disruption (MPSD) for 2 h/day for 3 consecutive days. Behavioral assessments included the open-field test for stress/anxiety and the Barnes maze for spatial learning and memory over three days. Hippocampal BDNF levels were quantified using ELISA. Intraperitoneal Ginkgo biloba extract improved learning in sleep-disrupted rats, reducing probe-day latency from 71 ± 11 s (deprived) to 38 ± 8 s (p < 0.001); Ginkgo biloba alone yielded 15 ± 8 s. The open-field test revealed a significant increase in both locomotor speed and total distance traveled in the sleep-disrupted rats compared with the other experimental groups (P < 0.001). Sleep disruption reduced hippocampal BDNF from 544.55 ± 23-381.19 ± 17 pm/ml (p < 0.0001). Ginkgo biloba treatment significantly prevented this reduction (557 ± 27 pm/ml; p < 0.001) and, when administered alone, increased BDNF by 20% compared to controls (653 ± 25 pm/ml). Sleep disruption impaired memory and learning but did not significantly affect anxiety. Treatment with Ginkgo biloba extract (250 mg/kg) improved memory and reduced anxiety. Hippocampal BDNF changes suggest restorative effects may be mediated by increasing BDNF levels reduced by deprivation. As an Iranian Ginkgo biloba extract was used, further research is needed to identify optimal extraction methods and phytochemical compositions for enhancing BDNF levels, thereby optimizing therapeutic potential of Ginkgo biloba -derived compounds for sleep and cognitive applications.

papers.title: A Neuro-Inspired Dual-Pathway Attention Network for EEG-Based Identity Recognition.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals have shown promise for biometric recognition due to their intrinsic liveness detection. However, their practical deployment remains limited. The main obstacles are non-stationary drift, scarce labeled data, and fluctuating signal quality. Most existing models adopt static computation graphs, which are ill-equipped to handle these variations. We propose a dual-pathway architecture that separates a data-driven bottom-up perceptual extractor from a prior-guided top-down modulator. A quality-aware gate computes instantaneous signal stability from channel-wise and temporal variances. It dynamically fuses the two pathways: bottom-up features dominate when the signal is clean, and identity priors take over when noise is high. Deep residual connections and pyramid fusion stabilize multi-scale learning. On the DEAP dataset, our method achieves 93.8% accuracy, which is 5.3 percentage points higher than the best baseline. On THU-EP, it reaches 97.2%. In cross-session tests on the noisy SEED-IV dataset, performance drops only 2.5% in Session 2 and 5.2% in Session 3. With only 1% of the training data on THU-EP, the model still attains 76.8% accuracy. Dynamic, signal-dependent fusion improves accuracy, cross-session robustness, and data efficiency. This work offers a practical, low-enrollment solution for patient identity verification, electronic health record access, and brain-computer interface authentication in clinical and mobile settings. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/cangtianhaoxue/ DPRAN.git.

papers.title: Genome-wide analyses identify 147 loci associated with obstructive sleep apnea
papers.abstract: The genetic components underlying obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted the largest GWAS meta-analysis (OSA; Ncases= 232,292; Ncontrols= 1,259,390) using European ancestry genetic data from five countries. We identified 147 independent loci and estimated SNP-based heritability at 16%. We report six independent loci in a separate African population meta-analysis (Ncases= 46,834; Ncontrols= 149,192). Spatially resolved gene enrichment in neural circuits involved synaptic transmission, including GABAergic and glutamatergic signalling, and cytoskeletal remodelling. OSA-derived polygenic risk scores predicted clinician-ascertained OSA status, Fitbit-derived sleep features, and symptom-based OSA risk and snoring in participants of diverse ancestral backgrounds. We identified putative causal relationships with ADHD, depression, multisite chronic pain, body mass index, and schizophrenia, among others. Our findings demonstrate a substantial genetic component underlying OSA risk beyond shared genetic effects with body mass index, implicating neurobiological pathways related to synaptic function and corticothalamic feedback loops.

papers.title: Feature processing for single-trial semantic decoding from EEG: a factorial comparison with pre-registered replication
papers.abstract: Single-trial decoding of semantic processing from EEG is used in cognitive neuroscience, brain-computer interfaces and EEG-to-text research. Because single trials are noisy, the choice of features can determine how much information a decoder uses. Yet these fields use different features that have not been compared systematically: event-related potential studies decode the voltage time course (the waveform), EEG-to-text studies mostly the power of oscillations in frequency bands. We crossed four feature-processing choices--signal representation (waveform or band power), time window, normalization and channel set--into 640 configurations and decoded whether a stimulus fitted its semantic context in three tasks: visual word pairs, objects in visual scenes, and words in spoken sentences (40 participants per task). Eleven pre-specified comparisons were tested jointly. The signal representation had by far the largest effect on accuracy (mean generalized eta squared = 0.165, an order of magnitude above any other effect). Averaged over tasks and other choices, balanced accuracy was 56.6% with the waveform and 50.6% with theta-band power (chance, 50%), and adding band power to the waveform lowered accuracy by 1.8 percentage points, in every task. Both effects replicated, and were larger, in a pre-registered study of 283 new participants from three sites. Neither a finer time-frequency decomposition including the delta band (2-4 Hz) nor a different way of combining power with the waveform changed this conclusion, whereas the time window, normalization and channel set mattered little. For semantic decoding from single EEG trials, the waveform carries the information, and band power does not add to it.

papers.title: Environmental enrichment enhances hepatic oxidative stress and antioxidant defenses without modulating immunometabolic gene expression in adult male mice.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment (EE) is a non-pharmacological intervention based on modifications of the housing environment that increase sensory, cognitive, and motor stimulation, and it has been proposed to modulate immunometabolic responses. To investigate the effects of EE on hepatic redox status, oxidative balance, and immunometabolic gene expression in healthy mice. Male C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned at 45 days of age to a standard environment (SE; n = 7) or an enriched environment (EE; n = 7) for six weeks. The EE group was housed in larger cages containing (tunnels, nesting material, and objects changed weekly). After euthanasia, liver samples were analyzed by spectrophotometric assays for NAD ⁺ /NADH, lipid peroxidation (TBARS), protein carbonylation, antioxidant enzyme activities (SOD, CAT, GST), GSH/GSSG ratio, and total sulfhydryl groups. Hepatic expression of inflammatory, metabolic, and mitochondrial genes was assessed by RT-qPCR (n = 4 per group). EE was associated with lower hepatic NAD⁺ (p = 0.001) and higher NADH (p = 0.006), lower lipid peroxidation (p = 0.004) and protein carbonylation (p = 0.009), and higher antioxidant enzyme activities. The GSH/GSSG ratio (p = 0.04) and sulfhydryl content (p = 0.001) were also higher. No significant changes were observed in the expression of the genes analyzed. Six weeks of EE were associated with changes in hepatic redox status, with lower oxidative damage markers and higher antioxidant defenses, without detectable changes in the expression of the genes analyzed. These findings suggest that short-term EE optimizes hepatic redox balance and antioxidant defenses, while noting that future studies with extended exposure and pathological models will clarify its long-term transcriptional and structural impacts.

papers.title: EEG biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases: Machine learning applications and clinical trial insights.

Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) have further enabled automated diagnosis, disease monitoring, and prognostic modelling using EEG data. Spectral power, event-related potentials, and connectivity are the main features, with support vector machines and neural networks as the primary classifiers. We review clinical trials involving EEG in NDs and highlight open-source EEG repositories to support reproducibility and data sharing. Despite promising results, challenges such as small sample sizes, methodological differences, limited model interpretability, and gaps in clinical validation remain. The review highlights the potential of EEG combined with ML/AI for early diagnosis and therapy, while outlining future directions through standardised pipelines, explainable models, and collaborative open data initiatives.

papers.title: Circadian misalignment reshapes gut microbial rhythms to underlie digestive disorders.
papers.abstract: Daily oscillations generated by the host circadian clock, together with rhythmic processes arising from the gut microbiota, form an integrated temporal framework that shapes digestive physiology. The host circadian clock shapes the gastrointestinal landscape through coordinated regulation of feeding patterns, epithelial renewal, immune surveillance, and bile acid metabolism. In turn, the gut microbiota generates rhythmic metabolites that provide reciprocal feedback to epithelial, metabolic, and immune pathways, further reinforcing circadian organization. Disruption of this bidirectional alignment, whether caused by altered light exposure, irregular eating patterns, genetic variation, or lifestyle-induced circadian misalignment, can fragment microbial oscillations, weaken mucosal resilience, and increase susceptibility to inflammatory, metabolic, and malignant digestive disorders. In this Review, we synthesize emerging insights into the molecular architecture that coordinates host and microbial rhythms and examine how its breakdown contributes to gastrointestinal disease. We also discuss chronobiological interventions, including feeding schedules, pharmacological timing, and microbiota-targeted strategies, that aim to restore temporal alignment. papers.title: Digital Phenotyping of Behavioral Instability as an Early Detection of Clinically Relevant Deterioration in Mental Health: Prospective Observational Multicenter Study.
papers.abstract: Early detection of clinically relevant changes remains a major challenge in mental health, as deterioration unfolds through subtle alterations in daily functioning. Advances in digital phenotyping and smartphone-based monitoring offer new opportunities to capture real-world settings. However, existing approaches rely on active self-reports, and few studies have examined whether within-person instability in passively sensed behavior can anticipate clinically recorded relapse events across diagnoses. This study aimed to adapt and evaluate an algorithm detecting behavioral changes associated with deterioration using passively collected smartphone data from a prospective, multicenter project investigating smartphone-based behavioral monitoring in adults with mental health conditions, to evaluate its performance in-sample and examine whether instability in behavioral patterns can serve as an early marker of relapse. We conducted a prospective, observational, multicenter study including 92 adult participants with mental health conditions (bipolar disorder, personality disorder, substance use disorder, and dual pathology) recruited from 2 specialized mental health centers in Madrid, Spain. Passive behavioral data, including physical activity, mobility, phone use, sleep, and daily routine indicators, were collected using a mobile app over periods ranging from 1 month to 1 year (mean follow-up of 123, SD 94.85 days). Behavioral profiles were generated using heterogeneous mixture models, and changes in behavioral stability were detected using a Bayesian online change-point detection approach. Model hyperparameters and source combinations were selected by grid search and heuristic exploration, and performance was evaluated in-sample by comparing detected change points with relapse events recorded in the electronic health record, using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Forty relapse events with available passive data were included in the analysis. The best-performing model achieved a mean in-sample area under the curve of 82.99% (SD 2.49%). At a false positive rate (FPR) of 5%, the model reached an average true positive rate (TPR) of 40.12% (95% CI 36.61%-43.63%), increasing to 61.10% (95% CI 56.42%-65.79%) at 10% FPR. Model performance was influenced by the temporal aggregation parameter, with optimal results obtained using minimal accumulation of past observations. Multimodal combinations integrating sleep, activity, and routine structure achieved the highest performance. These operating points correspond to decision thresholds matched at the specified FPR values, and the reported intervals reflect variability across 10 stochastic reruns on the same dataset rather than out-of-sample generalization. Performance showed run-to-run variability (maximum TPR of 53.58% vs mean TPR of 40.12%, SD 5.66% at 5% FPR), indicating limited stability. Behavioral instability shows preliminary potential for the early detection of behavioral changes associated with clinically relevant deterioration. Because hyperparameters, source combinations, and thresholds were tuned on the same events used for evaluation, the performance should be interpreted as an in-sample estimate, and external validation is required before clinical application.

papers.title: EEG and fNIRS evidence for brain responses to three tannins: implications for astringency surface sub-quality in red wine.
papers.abstract: The astringency surface sub-quality is pivotal to red wine perception, yet its neural bases remain unclear. The approaches of non-invasive neurophysiological techniques, sensory analysis, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis, and molecular docking were applied to examine the astringency surface sub-quality responses to three tannins-tannic acid, grape tannin and wine tannin-standardized to equivalent astringency intensity. The results showed that the three tannins at iso-intensity evoked distinct brain activity and sensory responses (wine tannin > tannic acid > grape tannin). The electroencephalography (EEG) results showed that frontal activation was significantly higher than in other regions, with differential delta-band power, while functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) revealed corresponding changes in oxygenated hemoglobin across different frontal cortical regions, most prominently at channel 6 in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex. LC-MS analysis of tannins indicated that higher levels of tannin oligomers, polymeric pigments and free anthocyanins were associated with finer astringency sub-quality and stronger neurophysiological responses. By establishing a clear link between chemical composition and neural activation, this investigation demonstrates the efficacy of using neurophysiological measures as a robust, objective tool to complement and refine traditional sensory evaluation of wine.

papers.title: Standards to Support Healthy Sleep for Pediatric Inpatients and Their Families: A Delphi Survey.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for physical and mental health. However, its importance is often overlooked in hospitals, negatively impacting children's well-being and recovery as well as their caregivers' ability to provide support. The aim of this study was to achieve consensus on internationally relevant standards to promote healthy sleep in hospitals providing pediatric in-patient care. An expert steering group developed 32 potential standards for supporting child and caregiver sleep in hospitals based on research, clinical experience, and surveys of pediatric sleep groups. A panel formed from the International Pediatric Sleep Association (IPSA) membership completed a 3-round Delphi study to guide the development of 5 to 15 final standards. Consensus was defined as at least 80% agreement using a 4-point Likert scale. Narrative comments were incorporated. Seventy-six multiprofessional participants from 23 countries/regions consented to participate. A panel of 49 were selected, maximizing geographical and professional representation, to complete rounds 2 and 3, with 35 (71%) from 20 countries/regions and 23 (47%) from 13 countries/regions participating, respectively. Consensus was high throughout. The final round organized the information into 5 overarching standards encompassing sleep included in the health care plan, commitment from senior management, promotion of circadian rhythms, family support, and environmental modifications. Each standard had 5 or 6 associated criteria. The standards achieved 96% agreement. Consensus was achieved on 5 overarching standards with their associated criteria designed to facilitate stepwise change, be adaptable to local contexts, and provide measurable outcomes to support healthy sleep for hospitalized children and families globally.

papers.title: 12-month trajectories of anxiety symptoms and functional recovery after new-onset stroke: A multicenter prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: The longitudinal course of poststroke anxiety remains poorly characterized. This study aimed to delineate the trajectories of anxiety symptoms within 12 months post-stroke and evaluate their associations with functional recovery. This prospective multicenter cohort study enrolled patients with new-onset stroke from 2018 to 2021. Anxiety symptoms were assessed using the 14-item Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA) at 2 weeks and at 3, 6, and 12 months. Latent class growth modeling and growth mixture modeling identified latent trajectory classes. Multivariate logistic regression evaluated the association between anxiety trajectory and 12-month functional outcome (modified Rankin scale). Among 1934 patients (1357 males; mean age 58.8 ± 10.9 years), the median initial HAMA score was 8 (4,13). Two distinct anxiety trajectories were identified: a low-decreasing group (1538 [79.5%]) with mild, descending symptoms (intercept, 8.400; mean difference, -3.510), and a high-increasing group (396 [20.5%]) characterized by escalating and persistent anxiety, with changes occurring predominantly within the first 3 months (intercept, 12.508; mean difference, 4.471). Female, moderate-to-severe stroke, depressive symptoms, poor sleep, and low resilience were independent risk factors of the high-increasing trajectory (all p < 0.01). Crucially, this trajectory was significantly associated with poor functional recovery at 12 months (aOR, 2.24; 99% CI, 1.58-3.17). A trajectory of increasing and persistent anxiety, identified in one-fifth of acute stroke patients, was independently associated with 12-month disability. These findings necessitate a paradigm shift from static, cross-sectional assessment to longitudinal tracking of anxiety symptoms, particularly during the first 3 months post-stroke, to improve functional outcomes.

papers.title: Individualized Atypicality of Structure-Function Configuration Marks Subthreshold Depression in Adolescents
papers.abstract: Background: Subthreshold depression (StD) in adolescence represents a critical state preceding major depressive disorder, yet its neurobiological substrates remain poorly characterized. Conventional structure-function coupling rely on DTI tractography, which produces non-isomorphic matrices and unstable single-subject estimates, limiting their clinical utility. We developed a novel isomorphic and multi-omics framework to quantify individualized structure-function configurations and tested whether adolescents with StD show reproducible deviations from a group-mean reference in a validation sample. Methods: We integrated five structural (cortical thickness, mean curvature, sulcal depth, fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity) and five functional (ReHo, ALFF, CBF, local and global connectivity strength) features to construct regional SIND-FIND configurations using symmetric KL divergence in a discovery-validation design (N = 131). Individual typicality scores were defined as the correspondence between each participant's regional configuration profile and HC reference (Leave one out). The score has undergone parallel validations using conventional SC-FC coupling, molecular alignment (PET/AHBA), and behavioral correlations. Results: Group-mean configuration maps were spatially correlated across samples ({rho} = .93, pspin < .001). StD participants showed lower typicality than HC (F(1,94) = 8.73, p = .004); the conventional SC-FC comparison was not significant (F(1,92) = 3.31, p = .072). Regional differences involved frontoparietal and salience regions and aligned with PET (r = .55, pspin < .001) and AHBA (r = .47, pspin = .003) maps. After covariate adjustment, typicality correlated with SCL-90 ({rho} = -.262, q = .013), SDS ({rho} = -.234, q = .022), ISI ({rho} = -.296, q = .012) and PSQI ({rho} = -.288, q = .012; BH-FDR across five scales); coupling tracked depressive but not sleep symptoms (ISI {rho} = -.161, q = .124). Within validation StD participants, SCL-90 remained negatively associated with typicality ({rho} = -.42, p = .023). Conclusion: Our isomorphic, multimodal framework captures coordinated structures-function deviation in adolescent StD with greater group-effect sensitivity than conventional SC-FC coupling, together with regional specificity, molecular spatial alignment, and behavioral relevance. Configuration typicality, defined relative to an HC group-mean reference, may serve as an individual-level marker of organizational deviation during adolescence, pending larger, demographic stratified samples.

papers.title: Obstructive sleep apnea may exacerbate periodontitis via microbial dysbiosis: A preliminary translational exploratory study.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is characterized by recurrent airway obstruction and could lead to chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH). Its relationship with periodontitis and underlying biological mechanisms, however, remains unclear. This translational human observation and experimental animal study aims (1) to investigate whether OSA exacerbates periodontitis and (2) to explore potential microbial and metabolic mechanisms. In the clinical component, patients with stage II periodontitis were allocated into two groups: periodontitis without OSA (N-OSA + P) and periodontitis with OSA (OSA + P). Gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) was analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and untargeted metabolomics. In the experimental study, eight male Wistar rats with ligature-induced periodontitis (P) were randomly assigned to normoxia or CIH exposure. Micro-CT, histological staining, ELISA, and qRT-PCR were performed to assess alveolar bone loss and inflammation responses. Demographic parameters were comparable between clinical groups. The OSA + P group exhibited higher microbial richness and a distinct subgingival community structure, characterized by enrichment of Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium. 21 endogenous differential metabolites were identified, primarily related to glycerophospholipid metabolism, with significant microbe-metabolite correlations observed. In the animal model, CIH exposure was associated with increased alveolar bone loss, enhanced inflammatory marker expression, and altered microbial community structure compared with normoxic controls. The presence of sleep breathing disturbances, such as OSA, seems to exacerbate periodontitis most likely by CIH, which leads to microbial dysbiosis, and metabolic reprogramming within the periodontal microenvironment.

papers.title: Longitudinal ACC Alterations with Low-Dose Pregabalin in pBMS.
papers.abstract: Primary burning mouth syndrome (pBMS) is a chronic orofacial pain disorder in which the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) serves as a core node in descending pain modulation and central sensitization. Multiparametric MRI evidence for structural, metabolic, and functional abnormalities across ACC subregions remains limited. This single-arm, prospective longitudinal study characterized ACC subregional alterations in 38 patients with moderate-to-severe pBMS and 31 matched healthy controls. All patients received a standardized 4-wk low-dose pregabalin course, with clinical and neuroimaging measures reassessed posttreatment; 30 of 34 patients who completed the trial provided posttreatment MRI data. At baseline, pBMS patients exhibited elevated ACC Glx/Cr (median 2.51 vs 1.93, P = 0.021) and tNAA/Cr (median 1.97 vs 1.72, P = 0.050) ratios, reduced gray matter volume in the left medial superior frontal gyrus and left frontal pole, and decreased pregenual ACC (pgACC) and subgenual ACC (sgACC)-centered connectivity involving the left middle frontal gyrus and left inferior parietal lobule. Glx/Cr correlated positively with visual analog scale (VAS) scores and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores, and tNAA/Cr correlated negatively with VAS and Central Sensitization Inventory scores. After treatment, the mean VAS reduction was 3.28 points (intention to treat; ITT); 44.74% (ITT, n = 38) and 50.00% (per-protocol, n = 34) attained ≥50% pain relief. The median ACC Glx/Cr decreased from 2.51 to 1.85 (P = 0.008) and pgACC-centered functional connectivity increased, whereas regional gray matter volume-including the pre-existing deficits in the left medial superior frontal gyrus and left frontal pole-showed no significant longitudinal change. In conclusion, pBMS is characterized by metabolic and functional neuroimaging alterations within pgACC and sgACC that covary with symptomatic improvement under low-dose pregabalin, whereas structural deficits remain unchanged in the short term. These exploratory findings support the potential benefits of low-dose pregabalin and highlight pgACC and sgACC as promising regions of interest for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Wearable-measured 24-hour heart rate variability and neovascular age-related macular degeneration: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Objective To examine wearable heart rate measures in age-related macular degeneration (AMD), reporting an exploratory observation in neovascular AMD. Results This cross-sectional All of Us analysis used minute-level Fitbit heart rate from adults aged [≥]50 years with eye care records. Among the 55 participants with neovascular AMD, the mean date of complete Fitbit recording days fell a median of 1.9 years after the first neovascular AMD diagnosis code. The 7259 comparators had no AMD. The planned primary test, sleeping heart rate with any AMD, was not statistically significant (odds ratio [OR] per 10 beats/min, 1.12; 95% CI, 0.97-1.29). Higher standard deviation of 5-minute average beat intervals (SDANN), a secondary measure, was associated with higher odds of neovascular AMD versus no AMD (OR per 10 ms, 1.12 [95% CI, 1.04-1.21], uncorrected P = 0.002, Bonferroni-adjusted P = 0.051 for 22 comparisons). In an exploratory comparison with non-neovascular AMD, the OR was 1.20 (95% CI, 1.08-1.32). After 24-hour heart rate adjustment, the OR versus no AMD was 1.13 (95% CI, 1.04-1.24). No associations were detected for epiretinal membrane or cataract. This exploratory observation warrants testing in recordings preceding conversion.

papers.title: Interrater agreement of seizure onset and spread in scalp EEG
papers.abstract: Objective. Faster seizure spread on intracranial EEG has been linked to worse surgical outcome. If contralateral spread on scalp EEG carried similar prognostic information, it could identify poor resection candidates before intracranial monitoring and direct them toward neuromodulation sooner. Testing this first requires that experts reliably annotate spread on scalp EEG. The interrater agreement for seizure spread detection on scalp EEG is unknown; prior scalp EEG reliability studies have focused mainly on seizure detection. We quantified expert agreement on the laterality, channels, and timing of seizure onset and contralateral spread. Methods. We retrospectively analyzed 79 seizures from 48 patients undergoing presurgical evaluation at a single center. Three board certified epileptologists independently marked the time and channels of onset and contralateral spread for each seizure. We measured agreement on onset laterality and spread presence with Gwet k, channels with Cohen k, and timing with the median absolute deviation (MAD). Interrater and majority vote consensus agreement were estimated with patient-clustered CIs. Results. Onset laterality showed substantial interrater agreement (Gwet k = 0.73, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.83); most disagreement involved bilateral onsets. Contralateral spread agreement was comparable (0.63, 0.48 to 0.76). Channel level agreement was higher for onset (inter rater Cohen k = 0.57) than for spread (0.38). Onset timing was highly consistent (median MAD 0.40 s); spread timing agreement was also high (1.99 s), but less so than onset timing (sign rank p < 0.001). Agreement did not differ across annotators or between temporal and non-temporal epilepsy. Significance. Epileptologists generally agree on onset laterality and whether and when seizures spread contralaterally, although spread channels are identified less reliably. These findings support the feasibility of measuring scalp EEG spread as a candidate noninvasive marker of seizure network extent. The public annotated dataset provides a multi-expert reference standard for developing automated spread detection algorithms.

papers.title: Filgotinib Safety Profile: A Pharmacovigilance Study Using Data from the VigiBase and Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System.
papers.abstract: Although filgotinib was approved in Europe and Japan, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) withheld approval owing to concerns about testicular toxicity. To address this gap, we conducted a pharmacovigilance study of filgotinib-related adverse drug reactions (ADRs). This study evaluated the safety profile of filgotinib using data from the VigiBase and FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) databases from the first quarter (Q1) of 2017 to Q1 2025. Signal detection involved calculating four disproportionality measures: the proportional reporting ratio (PRR), reporting odds ratio (ROR), information component (IC), and empirical Bayes geometric mean (EBGM), using predefined quantitative thresholds. Signals were refined using OpenVigil 2.1 to account for concomitant medications. The signals were ordered according to their IC025 values rather than PRR value. Analysis of VigiBase data (2207 reports) revealed a predominance of ADRs among female patients (74.8%) and individuals aged 45-64 years (38.1%). Notably, 95% of reports originated in Europe. Strong disproportionate reporting signals were identified for lower respiratory tract infection (PRR = 20.5 [χ2 = 1002.3], lower bound [LB] ROR = 16, IC025 = 3.7, EBGM05 = 15.6) and hypercholesterolemia (PRR = 29.8 [χ2 = 611.9], LB ROR = 19.8, IC025 = 3.5, EBGM05 = 19.5). Time-to-onset analysis revealed diverse onset times (median, 1 month), with most ADRs assessed as possibly related to filgotinib. In FAERS (190 reports), disproportionate reporting signals were observed for epididymitis (PRR = 1060.3 [χ2 = 8350.6], LB ROR = 544.1, IC025 = 2.9, EBGM05 = 512.0) and sleep apnea syndrome (PRR = 62.7 [χ2 = 486.0], LB ROR = 32.3, IC025 = 2.6, EBGM05 = 30.8). This pharmacovigilance study identified several disproportionality signals, including epididymitis, sleep apnea syndrome, infections, and metabolic abnormalities, warranting continued clinical vigilance and further investigation of the safety profile of filgotinib.
